title: Nepal suspends search after 16 swept away by avalanche - The Indian Panorama
description: Nepal suspends search after 16 swept away by avalanche  The Indian Panorama
publisher.title: The Indian Panorama
full_article:
KATHMANDU (TIP): Dire weather has forced Nepal to suspend search operations after a Himalayan avalanche caused what is feared to be the worst expedition disaster in over a decade, the National Mountain Guide Association said.

Since the avalanche swept through the base camp of the 7,126-metre (23,345-foot) Himlung peak early on Sunday, four bodies have been recovered while 12 people remain missing.

“The conditions are very challenging,” said Tul Singh Gurung, president of the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association. “The search has been paused”.

The 12 missing people are all Nepali workers preparing for later expeditions on Himlung, near the Chinese border, a popular destination for mountaineers looking to begin climbing 7,000-metre peaks.

Rescue team leader Mingma G Sherpa said he had little hope of finding the missing alive.

“Looking at the bodies recovered, it would be impossible for the rest to survive,” he told AFP. “The scale of the avalanche is massive, we can go back when the snow melts a bit.”

The team of eight mountain guides had reached the base camp on Sunday evening to begin the search, digging through more than four metres (14 feet) of snow.

Tents were buried under deep snow.

The bodies of two mountain guides were recovered on Sunday, and those of two kitchen staff were pulled out earlier this week.

Nepal’s worst mountaineering disasters in recent years occurred in 2014, when an avalanche killed 16 people on Everest, and in 2015, when an earthquake killed 18 people, also on Everest.

Nepal is still searching for bodies from devastating floods sparked by a mountain glacial collapse on August 26 that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 6,000 missing.

Heavy rain since Thursday has triggered other floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the national disaster agency.

Home to eight of the world’s 14 highest peaks, Nepal relies heavily on mountaineering and trekking tourism.

title: Hundreds missing, including 47 Americans, in deadly Nepal floods, local officials say - abcnews.com
description: Hundreds missing, including 47 Americans, in deadly Nepal floods, local officials say  abcnews.com
publisher.title: abcnews.com
full_article:
Serious flash flooding in Nepal on Wednesday morning has left over a hundred reported dead and hundreds more missing, including at least 47 American tourists, Nepali officials said, after a massive wall of water tore through a region on the Nepal-Tibet border.

The flooding, captured in dramatic video footage, occurred in the northern Rasuwa district, along the border with Tibet, at around 8:40 a.m. local time on Wednesday, authorities said, inundating coastal areas along the Trishuli River, burying some buildings and damaging bridges and roadways.

In a statement, Nepal's office of the prime minister expressed "deep sorrow" over the loss of life. "Offering heartfelt tribute to all those who lost their lives in this natural disaster, it extends its sincere condolences to the bereaved families and relatives," the statement shared on social media said.

Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a victim of flash flooding to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo

Related Deadly Nepal flood caused by enormous landslide, glacier tumble: Scientist

The prime minister's office later said search and rescue operations carried out by the Nepali Army would continue through the night.

Nepali police said 162 were killed in the flood-affected areas, while Chinese state-run media Xinhua News Agency reported three dead. Authorities said the identification process is ongoing.

A resident walks along a street covered in mud following flash floods and a landslide disaster in Devghat, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, August 26, 2026. Prakash Mathema/AFP via Getty Images

At least 403 foreign nationals and 93 Nepali tourists are reported missing, according to the Prime Minister's Office of Nepal. Chinese media reported 265 missing.

The Nepali Tourism Board reported that the missing includes at least 47 American tourists who have been out of contact since floods hit the Rasuwa region.

The State Department said the number of Americans among the missing and otherwise impacted by the floods has fluctuated throughout the day, and that officials don’t yet have an accurate figure.

A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 27, 2026. Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

"The United States extends its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the devastating flash floods in the Rasuwa district of Nepal. Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster," a department spokesperson said in a statement issued later Wednesday.

The spokesperson said the State Department is "closely monitoring the situation and is deploying a disaster response advisor to the region to support response efforts. The Department will also provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services, supporting emergency shelter, relief items, and water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities."

Houses lie partially submerged in muddy water along a riverside after flash floods at Trishuli Bazar in Nepal's Nuwakot district on August 26, 2026. A massive flood swept through Nepal's northern Rasuwa district on August 26, damaging roads and power infrastructure as authorities scrambled to assess the scale of the destruction. Prabin Ranabhat/AFP via Getty Images

An influential Indian spiritual guru and entrepreneur known as Sadhguru said in a post on social media that 77 people who were on tours organized by his Isha Foundation were at an immigration center at the Nepal-Tibet border when the floodwaters came rushing in. Isha Foundation has confirmed to ABC News that 22 of the 77 people are Americans.

Rescuers gather on a rooftop as floodwaters sweep through Trishuli Bazar following a flash flood, in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Narendra Shrestha/EPA/Shutterstock

Many of them were traveling to or from Mount Kailash, a Himalayan peak near the border between Nepal and Tibet, an autonomous region of China. Mount Kailash, which is part of a Hindu pilgrimage called the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, is revered by many Hindus as the spiritual home of the god Shiva.

The Isha Foundation, which is headquartered in India, also has a base in McMinnville, Tennessee. The group's coordinator told ABC News the group has been in touch with family members in the U.S.

Popular Reads Christa Pike unconscious and on ventilator after botched execution: Attorneys 3 hours ago Tel Aviv flight drops thousands of feet after pilot stabbed in alleged terror attack Sep 30 District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Sep 29

Three of the missing Americans were listed as traveling with a Nepali company called Fishtail Tours and Travel. The agency confirmed to ABC News that three American nationals are among the missing tourists traveling with them.

A drove view of mud covered properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters

Efforts to locate and rescue the missing tourists are ongoing, the company said, without providing any further information on their possible whereabouts or well-being.

The Nepal Tourism Board said that local tourism and law enforcement authorities were "working to verify the whereabouts and safety status of tourists and travelers who were in or traveling through the affected areas."

Nepali authorities have mobilized 656 police personnel to respond as of 7:30 p.m. local time, according to police.

A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. Reuters

The flood was reportedly triggered by a landslide about 20 kilometers northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border post along the Nepal-China border, according to Nepal Disaster Management.

A 5.2-magnitude landslide impacted Nepal on Wednesday, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.

The seismic activity from the landslide was initially erroneously reported as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake, the agency said. It is unclear what triggered the landslide.

A geophysicist at New York's Columbia University told ABC News it appeared a landslide in the Himalayas took away a large glacier or parts of a glacier in the mountain pass.

The U.S. Embassy in Kathmandu said in posts to X that it was "deeply saddened by the tragic loss of life and devastation" caused by the flooding. "We are closely tracking developments and remain in close contact with Nepali authorities," the embassy said.

Also among the foreign nationals listed as missing in the Tourism Board's preliminary count were Indian, Malaysian, British, South African, Dutch and Australian tourists.

A boy looks at the devastation caused by flash flooding along the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Aug. 26, 2026. Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo

Three army helicopters attempted to fly in to conduct relief operations Wednesday but had to turn back due to bad weather between Kathmandu, Nepal and the flooded areas, Sunil Sharma, spokesperson at Nepal Tourism Board, told ABC News.

Authorities are working to identify victims and conduct rescue efforts, and they hope rescue flights can resume tomorrow if the weather improves, Sharma said.

full_article:
Tennis does not yet command the mass audience that cricket enjoys in Nepal, but its footprint is becoming much easier to see. Kathmandu regularly hosts international junior competition, Nepali players are appearing in events abroad, and youth programmes are connecting the country to the wider Asian tennis pathway. Rather than one dramatic breakthrough, tennis in Nepal is developing through tournaments, individual players, coaching and a gradually expanding audience.

Nepal’s Place on the International Tennis Calendar

One of the clearest signs of progress is Nepal’s presence in International Tennis Federation competition. Kathmandu hosted two J60 junior tournaments in early 2026, giving young players the chance to compete for ranking points on home courts. Nepal also hosted South Asian qualifying for the ITF Asia 12 & Under Team Competition in Lalitpur in April, bringing junior teams from across the region together and giving local players valuable international match experience.

For fans, international tennis is also one of the easiest sports to follow statistically. A match can be broken down through rankings, recent results, surface, head-to-head history and tournament draws. Betting markets add another layer of numbers, but odds should be treated as market prices rather than predictions. Someone using a best betting app to compare tennis markets should still check the draw, playing surface, recent workload and player news before interpreting a line.

Players Give Nepali Tennis a Visible International Story

Individual players matter enormously in a developing tennis scene because they give younger athletes a pathway they can actually see. Abhishek Bastola has represented Nepal internationally, competed in the Davis Cup and continued playing events abroad in 2026. Fans following a tournament through a MelBet betting app or another live-score service can use the same basic information that matters to tennis analysis everywhere: current form, opponent level, surface and recent match volume.

Junior players are also giving Nepal more visibility around Asia. In 2026, Nepali juniors competed in ITF pathways and international events outside the country. Shivali Gurung, for example, reached the girls’ doubles title at the J60 Colombo event in September. Results like these are important because junior tennis is where ranking experience, travel routines and exposure to different playing styles begin to accumulate.

Youth Tennis Is the Foundation of Long-Term Growth

Tennis development starts well before a player reaches the Davis Cup or the professional circuit. Nepal’s recent hosting of junior international events shows why a local pathway matters: young athletes need regular matches, coaching, competitive courts and opportunities to face players from other countries.

Junior tournaments: ITF events in Kathmandu allow Nepali players to gain international experience without every competition requiring overseas travel.

Regional competition: South Asian qualifying events expose young players to opponents from neighbouring tennis systems.

Coaching and practice: Consistent technical training is especially important in a sport where movement, serve mechanics and point construction develop over years.

International pathways: Strong junior results can lead toward higher-level ITF events, college opportunities and eventually professional competition.

This structure does more than produce elite players. Regular junior competition gives families, coaches and local clubs a reason to stay involved, while international events create measurable goals for developing athletes. For Nepal, the challenge is not simply discovering one exceptional player but making the route from beginner to competitive tennis more consistent.

Recent Tennis Highlights in Nepal

Nepal’s 2026 tennis calendar offered several useful signs of activity. Kathmandu hosted back-to-back J60 junior tournaments from late January into early February, while Lalitpur staged the South Asian qualifying event for the ITF Asia 12 & Under Team Competition in April. These events put Nepali courts directly into the regional development system rather than leaving local players dependent only on domestic competition.

At the senior level, Abhishek Bastola remained one of the most visible Nepali players internationally in 2026. He competed abroad on professional and UTR circuits while preparing for major regional competition. His experience also highlights one of the difficulties facing tennis in Nepal: international travel, coaching, equipment and tournament entry create costs that can be much harder to absorb in an individual sport than in a centrally funded team programme.

Courts, Phones and Streams: How Fans Follow Tennis

Tennis is well suited to digital viewing because matches generate a constant stream of useful information. Fans can move between live scores, draws, rankings, highlights and short match clips without needing to watch every point. Grand Slam events and major ATP and WTA tournaments also give Nepali viewers a global entry point into the sport, while local and regional competitions make that interest more relevant at home.

Social media can help close the visibility gap between major international stars and Nepali players. Tournament results, training clips and junior achievements can circulate quickly, giving athletes exposure even when traditional television coverage is limited. For a smaller tennis market, that digital layer is particularly important because it keeps the sport visible between the relatively few major events held in Nepal.

Where Tennis in Nepal Can Go Next

The future of Nepali tennis depends less on a sudden popularity boom than on continuity. Hosting ITF junior tournaments, strengthening coaching, maintaining usable courts and helping talented players compete internationally can gradually deepen the sport’s base. Nepal already has an official national association within the international tennis structure and has shown that it can host regional and junior events. If those opportunities become more regular, tennis can build a stronger identity alongside Nepal’s larger sports. The most useful signs will be practical ones: more juniors playing ranked events, more Nepali athletes travelling competitively, better access to coaching and a calendar that gives players meaningful matches throughout the year.

The Nepal government is planning to drain four high-altitude glacial lakes to reduce the risk of floods downstream, as it moves to strengthen safeguards against potential glacial lake outburst floods, Reuters reported.

The move follows a deadly disaster in Nepal's border region with China, where a glacier collapse unleashed landslides and a flash flood, leaving more than 1,400 people dead. Rescuers are still searching for more than 5,000 people reported missing.

Nepal has experience in managing the risks posed by glacial lakes, having lowered the water level of Tsho Rolpa by around three metres in 2000. Similar risk-reduction measures were implemented at Imja Lake, near Mount Everest, roughly a decade later.

The proposed $50-million project will focus on Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho and Hongu II, four glacial lakes located in central and eastern Nepal. Design work and detailed studies are scheduled to begin during the fiscal year ending in mid-July 2027.

“Our aim is to lower the risk of the lakes breaching their natural dams and reduce the risk of downstream floods,” Subash Tuladhar, an expert at Nepal's Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research, told Reuters.

The project envisages controlled drainage through canals and gated structures that would release water into nearby rivers. However, officials said the work would involve considerable logistical and safety challenges because of the extreme altitude and the risk of sudden flooding.

Sanjeeb Baral, executive director of the research centre, said the actual drainage work would begin after detailed studies and could take as long as six years.

The project will also include the installation of monitoring sensors, flood forecasting and early-warning systems, as well as measures to improve the resilience of downstream communities. The latest disaster has added urgency to Nepal's efforts to manage glacial lake risks.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the United Nations last month that retreating glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and increasingly unpredictable rivers were imposing a heavy cost on the country despite Nepal's relatively low greenhouse-gas emissions.

Nepal has recorded around 26 glacial lake outburst flood events over the past four decades. Extreme climate-related events kill more than 300 people and cause millions of dollars in damage in the country each year, according to officials.

Samjwal Ratna Bajracharya, a retired ICIMOD expert, said lowering the identified lakes by around three metres could substantially reduce the risk of a catastrophic outburst.

He said the lakes are expanding rapidly and could breach because of earthquakes, avalanches, changing climatic conditions or human activity.

The factual basis of the main development is consistent with the Reuters report: Nepal plans studies for draining the four lakes, with the project potentially taking up to six years and including warning and monitoring systems.

title: Nepal floods: A deepening crisis - Islamic Relief Worldwide
description: Nepal floods: A deepening crisis  Islamic Relief Worldwide
publisher.title: Islamic Relief Worldwide
full_article:
October 2, 2026 Nepal -

More than a month on from the deadly floods and the humanitarian crisis in Nepal continues to deepen.

More rainfall in September has further worsened conditions for displaced families in the worst affected districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot. Temporary shelters have been damaged, leaving already vulnerable families exposed to the elements.

At least 1,450 people are now confirmed to have been killed by the floods. More than 5,000 people are still missing and unaccounted for.

Worsening conditions

Displaced families are now facing critical food shortages as emergency food rations run out. Damaged farmland and ruined livelihoods mean that the growing hunger crisis is likely to last well into 2027.

Islamic Relief’s emergency response manager in Nepal, Laxmi Raj Joshi, elaborated:

“Whole communities remain displaced and their income and homes are gone. Within a second, they lost their household, their livelihood, their land and stores. Now they are in a deepening financial crisis.

“We are worried that in the coming weeks the food crisis will be alarming. Emergency food rations have been used, and people don’t have money to buy more.

“At the same time, thousands of people remain in temporary shelters and face growing risks as winter approaches. Continued support is urgently needed to prevent hunger, secure safe shelter and begin rebuilding their lives with dignity.”

Islamic Relief have reached around 12,000 people in northern Nepal with vital humanitarian assistance

Expanded support

Some communities remain isolated due to the damaged roads, meaning that the delivery of humanitarian aid is still complicated more than a month after the disaster.

Approximately 85,000 people in Nepal are need of humanitarian assistance.

Islamic Relief were on the scene within days of the crisis. We have so far provided emergency shelter assistance to nearly 3,000 families – around 200 families of that number also received food packages that will last for 2 weeks.

Over the next few weeks, Islamic Relief will deliver food packages and shelter kits to a further 275 affected families.

More is needed to help those still suffering. Please give generously to our Nepal Floods Emergency Appeal today.

title: Nepal Floods: Why Big Dams Can Deepen Disaster - Frontline Magazine
description: Nepal Floods: Why Big Dams Can Deepen Disaster  Frontline Magazine
publisher.title: Frontline Magazine
full_article:
The recent floods in Nepal killed over 1,400 people and destroyed thousands of homes. According to Daanish Mustafa, professor of critical geography at King’s College London, linking climate change to the disaster does nothing to shift the goal away from adapting meaningfully. He says the root of the crisis lies in the neocolonial mindset that infuses importance and pride to high-impact projects for grand outcomes and to commercial activities that cater to certain entrenched interests. Mustafa has spent much of his career researching water, hazards, and the relationship between landscapes and human development in South Asia. Edited excerpts: What are your thoughts on the recent floods in Nepal? How much damage could have been avoided through better planning, infrastructure and disaster preparedness? The Nepal flood happened in a very small catchment. It was basically a glacial slip that fell into a moraine, and then there was a wall of water that came down. Most people don’t remember the Chong Kumdan flood of 1929. That happened in the Shyok valley, in the Karakoram. And that flood caused the railway bridge in Attock to be swept away from a 15-20 metre-high wave, a thousand kilometres down from where the GLOF [glacial lake outburst flood] had happened. In the Karakoram, you end up having glaciers that are 100 times bigger than the Eastern Himalayan glaciers, and you have rivers that are 100 times bigger than the Eastern Himalayan rivers. Then, you’re building dams—the tallest dam in the world, 892 feet [272 m] high, the Diamer-Bhasha is being built. It’s 1,000 times bigger than any hydroelectric projects that you had in Nepal. So imagine a scenario of a wall like that coming down, taking out an 892-foot [272 m] high dam. Then there’s a Dasu dam downstream of it; it’ll take that out. Then it’ll take the Tarbela out. Then, it’ll take every piece of infrastructure out because every time you breach a structure, you further amplify the wave. There’s a nuclear reactor in Chashma, right by the river Indus, about 200-300 km downstream of Attock. If that goes, Pakistan will be uninhabitable for the next 50,000 years. Pakistan, Indian Punjab, and Kashmir. That’s the level of catastrophic scenario we are looking at. Also Read | Nepal floods: What went wrong and what’s next? What is changing in South Asia’s water systems? Are we seeing changes in the intensity, timing, or distribution of rainfall, riverflow, snow and glacial melt, also given climate change? Did the Nepal disaster happen because of climate change? Maybe it did, maybe it did not. But it doesn’t matter because the Karakoram and the Hindu Kush region is one of the most dynamic regions in the world: it is seismically active, there are earthquakes every day. There’s a plate going down which doesn’t care if there is climate change or not. Ice, glaciers, cryosphere: it’s a dynamic system. Glaciers move. Glaciers recede. Glaciers grow. Glaciers die out. Hydrologically, it’s the most dynamic mountain range in the world. You can take white man’s science and pretend that we control it, pretend that we know it, pretend that we can predict it. Your pretence has fallen apart. It never worked. The fact is that what you’re trying to do in the high Himalaya is just something that is foolhardy to try. There’s a reason that with the same neural density, with the same intellectual capacity, for thousands of years, South Asian societies said “We’re not going to mess with that stuff.” And in the last 150 years, the British came and they said, “We’re going to show you Brown people how our white science can do things that you never thought should be done.” And you’re reaping the consequences. When you start thinking about decolonising water, you’re talking about precisely that. The Christian missionaries always took science with them. They tried to undermine all the mythologies and the local knowledge of glaciers and mountains. I think that these tropes of climate change: how do you tell the difference? There are so many more people living in the flat plains. We have so much of a richer gauge network now to actually measure those things. The exposed populations are so much greater. Groundwater extraction is so much more. The extractivism is so much more intense. How do I separate out the climate signal from the political economy of why people are living where they are living? You can try, but to what effect? So what will that do? One of the political signals is that, “It’s not our fault.” The real estate people get off the hook and chase away poor people from their lands, from their livelihoods, and build these ghastly projects that will further constrict the channels and therefore further accentuate the flood peaks. A vehicle rides along the Nepal-China Highway near the Bhote Koshi River at Syabrubesi in Nepal's Rasuwa district on September 29, 2026, in the aftermath of the August 26 flash flood. | Photo Credit: PRAKASH MATHEMA/AFP How can large infrastructure in mountain regions amplify the consequences of floods, landslides and glacial hazards? How does a large dam accentuate the damage? In a couple of ways. The worst case scenario is that very few dams in the world—depending upon the size of the GLOF and what have you—can withstand the GLOF that we are doing. You’ve breached a lake, the storage of water broke and came right down. And then you come across another lake that you’ve built. And it is going to break that. When a boulder the size of two houses hits a dam, it’s going to go. And when it goes, you have created another GLOF. So that’s the obvious one way in which it makes things worse. The other one is that the lower dams like Mangla, Tarbela, and Bhakra Nangal, and others, what you do is you hold back a lot of silt within those dams. You also eliminate flood pulses. All rivers have a flood pulse. It’s monsoon season; the river’s going to flood; it is going to spread out on to the flood plain. What we have done is we have engineered a way to moderate floods with the dams and diversions. [By doing so we have] exchanged high-frequency, low-intensity events for low-frequency, high-intensity events. Every dam has a safe design capacity that it can take. The whole protocol for flood management is that infrastructure must not be lost. When a barrage’s safe design capacity is exceeded, they breach the right bank of the river and flood out the surrounding lands in order to protect the infrastructure, because if you don’t, then you lose the infrastructure. In the case of India, once the safe capacity of the dam is exceeded, that’s when you open all the gates. When Satluj and Ravi both open their gates, you get catastrophic damage. You just did in 2025. So when you build infrastructure, your priority is to protect the infrastructure. And you can never build an infrastructure which is completely flood-proof. You can’t, it’s just not possible. In the case of Pakistan, it is a standard operating procedure that all reservoirs should be as full as possible by August 20. In the past, we have seen that the flood peaks have happened in September, so when a flood peak comes down, it comes across a full reservoir, then if you don’t open the reservoir, you lose the reservoir. If you open up the reservoir, catastrophic damage happens downstream of it. Also, when you hold back the silt, what you’re doing is reducing channel capacity. For 5 to 10 years, you’ve not allowed floods to happen. What used to be a medium flood becomes a high flood, what becomes a high flood becomes a very high flood, and a very high flood becomes a catastrophic flood. That’s the bargain you have made with infrastructure. Does this trade-off come every time one builds a dam? Of course. Certainly, in South Asia. Our rivers drain the youngest mountains in the world. Hence, they carry the largest silt load in the world. So, large-dam building technology was fundamentally invented in Europe and North America. If you compare the Colorado River, which is the size of a minor tributary of the Ganges, and say, “They built a dam; why don’t we build a dam like that?” Or the Murray-Darling basin, if you’ve ever seen the Murray-Darling basin in Australia, you will be like, “You’re calling this a river?” We won’t even call it a stream in India. When you have the size of the kind of rivers that you have in South Asia, and when you consider the silt loads, they didn’t even understand what silt loads meant in the 1950s and 1960s when they were building these dams. Now we do. But all the textbooks in Indian and Pakistani engineering departments are written by dead white people who were studying these streams in North America and Europe, which has got nothing to do with us. The problems that we are seeing today are very much a function of the colonial mindset with colonial education. Lower dams, like the Bhakra-Nangal dam, hold back a lot of silt and eliminate flood pulses. | Photo Credit: Mrinal Pal/Getty Images What can governments do to make people better informed and better prepared, particularly at the local level? In the first instance, early warnings. But your early warning is your legacy colonial scientific system. Its articulation is in a language that no one understands. It makes them happy because they’ve given you an objective reality but it does nothing. First of all, make it vernacular. It has to be in terms that are understandable. India is gigantic. There’s local meteorology there. So for that, what you need to have is a denser network of registrations, involving more people in citizen meteorology. I’ve always made the case for Pakistan’s meteorological department—why can’t you have a $10 weather station on top of every government school in Pakistan? Children collect data so they understand the data. If people do it, they understand and believe it. In the context of Pakistan, what works in Balochistan doesn’t work in Punjab, what works in Punjab is not good for Gilgit-Baltistan. So it is context specific. Is the perception that environmental and construction regulations are weaker in the Global South than in the advanced countries a fair assessment? To what extent can regulatory failures turn natural hazards into large disasters? Is there no corruption in the Global North? Having lived in the Global North, I don’t see much of a difference. They just do it in English. How can local communities be involved in planning and in designing systems to predict and to prepare for these catastrophic events? Let me flip the question on its head. There’s a person sitting in Roorkee or in Kolkata or in Delhi planning a massive canal project in Gujarat. Goes there for four to five days, takes pictures, checks it out. Comes back, designs the whole thing. What stupefies me is that person is involved, but the person living there is not. The absurdity of it is that someone who has never [set] foot in a particular place has the right [to plan], and the people who are actually living there [and have] spent their whole lives there—their Gods are there, their mythologies, their spirituality, their identity, everything is there—do not. So the question itself is the answer in a manner of speaking. The biggest issue with rivers and flooding in the Indus basin is drainage. Once the water comes, you have to drain it. Which way does the drainage go? No engineer in the Pakistani irrigation department can tell you which way the drainage goes. The local people know. Even a child can tell you, “The water goes that way.” But that’s the person you don’t want to shake hands with. That’s the person you don’t want to listen to. So, to my mind, “how can the local community be involved” is a question that needs reflection. What if one were to ask, “How can engineers be involved?” That sounds like a more difficult question except that it’s the easiest one to answer. People walk on the dry riverbed of the Indus River in Hyderabad, Pakistan, April 24, 2025. | Photo Credit: YASIR RAJPUT/REUTERS How should governments reconcile the economic importance of agriculture and industry with the need for long-term water security? The largest exporter of embedded water in agricultural products in the world is Pakistan. Who benefits from sugarcane production? The exporters do. There’s a certain structure of subsidies that are offered to them. The highest incidence of malnourishment in Pakistan is in the irrigated districts. How can you have the highest level of per-capita malnourishment in the country in the regions which have the highest agricultural production? The answer is right there, because that land and that water is going towards the production of cash crops that benefit certain agro-capitalist interests exporting overseas or domestically. A poor person drawing water from a water well in rural Bengal is not an economic actor. Yet [multinational corporations] taking all that water away, packaging it and selling it to you [and] making millions in the process is an economic activity [and] beneficial for the country. That person’s dysentery, that person’s malnourishment is not a statistic that is of interest. Eight hundred million people in India depend upon the Indian government for ration for their food security. But that does not feature in the conversations. This is outrageous. So, I think if you buy into the parameters of a conversation or buy into the assumptions of the conversation, it takes you only in one direction—when you’re talking about economic growth and development and all the rest of it. If you talk about a different framework, you can change the parameters of the conversation. In many cities, some people have abundant access to water while others travel long distances for basic needs. What does a fair system of water allocation look like? There are children dying of renal failure in Karachi—80 per cent of the population of Karachi is water insecure. It turns out that there are about 25 golf courses in Karachi; one golf course takes up enough water for about 22,000 households. Half a kilometre from the [DHA Golf Club] is a child dying of renal failure because they are drinking saline water. That’s the water story of South Asia and in that story is everything that’s wrong with the development model. How should governments approach developments in wetlands, floodplains, mountain regions, and other landscapes? Every square centimetre of this planet is ecologically sensitive. There is some ecological cost that you have to bear. Ultimately, instead of getting into the idiom of ecology, why don’t we get into the idiom of human dignity or the idiom of livelihoods where there is clean drinking water in the spring? When you’re talking about a nice, clean forest, when you’re talking about healthy fisheries in a stream, you’re talking about the food security of the people who depend on the stream. An equitable, just society will have a robust ecology because that’s how people gain their livelihood, their food security, their cultural belonging, their dignity. So why worry about ecology, why not worry about dignity? When you start talking in those terms, then a different conversation emerges which takes everyone along. The closed gates of the Salal Dam on the Chenab river after the suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty, in Reasi district, Jammu and Kashmir, May 5, 2025. | Photo Credit: PTI How should governments decide between competing claims on water from households, agriculture, industry and emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence? I’m very sceptical of AI. They have very good uses in, say, engineering, medicine, in specific niche kinds of situations, and in the military. But if you are devoting stupefying amounts of water and land, taking it away from its other uses, urgent uses, you make funny cartoons and fake pictures and made-up term papers—no comedy or tragedy in the world could capture the sheer stupidity of it all. The second thing is: isn’t it funny that 70 per cent of the new energy demand in the United States is coming from data centres and AI? Do you really want to devote all of those resources to an algorithm? To what effect? Who is it benefiting? The elites don’t care for our people. Let not a man from Silicon Valley come over there, take away your land, take away your water, and suck up all the energy. That could be put to other uses. My view is: how do you decide? Don’t go there. Because this is all going to go bust. AI cannot work. Certainly not with the energy cost, let alone the water cost. Not one company will tell you how much energy goes into it. So once you understand it, it’s a fraud, don’t do it. Also Read | The human cost of conservation As we see water stress and extreme hydrological events, how important will transboundary cooperation become? It is essential. For example, I have been telling everyone in Pakistan that Pakistan should thank [Prime Minister Narendra] Modi for pulling out of the Indus Waters Treaty. When the Indus Waters Treaty was signed, in 1960, they did not understand silt. They did not understand surface and groundwater dynamics. The day we destabilise the capitalist model of agriculture, the sheer absurdity of fighting over water will become apparent. Because water is going to flow in that direction, it’s going to flow downhill no matter what you do. Eighty per cent of the crop-water requirement in Pakistan comes from groundwater, which is also true in Indian Punjab. So, the whole transboundary water conflict is basically an argument between gangsters: who gets to do the worst to the river. My submission to you is that that is a losing proposition. If we change the parameters of the conversation, then you’ll automatically find that the free and flowing river is to the benefit of India as it is to the benefit of Bangladesh. A free and flowing river is as much to the benefit of Nepal as it is to the benefit of India, in Bihar. How that will emerge is when you’re thinking about the lives and livelihoods of people who live by the river, not the fantasies of the engineers and planners in the capital. The problem is with them, the problem is not with the people. title: A Plan B First Ascent: Nepal Landslides Force Veteran Italians to Change Peaks - Explorersweb »
description: A Plan B First Ascent: Nepal Landslides Force Veteran Italians to Change Peaks  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
It’s become their custom: Nives Meroi and Romano Benet are back in Nepal to attempt a new route or a first ascent of a scarcely visited 6,000m peak. The recent landslides affecting the Manang region have forced them to change their destination, but not their ambitions.

Their original goal was a new route on the south face of 7,134m Tilicho, north of Annapurna. However, landslides caused by heavy rain last weekend have severely affected that region. The Italian couple, who always walk to their base camp, were unable to reach Tatopani, the starting point of the trek. Usually, the town is accessible by road, but now even footpaths are not possible.

“We were told there were 46 landslides along the route, and conditions of the path to base camp [beyond Tatopani] are unknown,” Meroi told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu.

Benet posted today that they have found an alternative goal, something they can reach on foot rather than by helicopter. Hiking in is part of the expedition for them, and they have no wish to change that.

Plan B: Jugal II

“We’ve decided to explore the Jugal Himal area, recently opened to climbers,” Benet wrote. “Information is scarce, but we’ve decided to attempt unclimbed Jugal II (6,518m).”

The main peaks of the Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

Meroi and Benet, who have both summited all the 8000’ers without supplemental oxygen, have also pioneered several new routes and first ascents. Meroi earned a Piolet d’Or for his climb of Kabru II in the Kangchenjunga region. For Jugal II, Tine Cuder of Slovenia has joined them as a third.

The Jugal Himal is quite close to Kathmandu, just northeast of town on the border with Tibet. It’s reachable by bus with a few days’ trekking, as Paul Ramsden explained when he opened a new route on Jugal Spire with Tim Miller. This climb also earned them a Piolet d’Or.

These peaks have been so rarely visited because until 2023, they were closed to climbing. That spring, Nepal opened Jugal I (6,591m) and Jugal II (6,518m), together with five other peaks in the area.

In spring 2024, veteran Um Hong-gil of South Korea launched a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi, to unclimbed Jugal I and Jugal II. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II, which remains unclimbed, according to The Himalayan Database.

Climbers, circled, on the final ridge of Jugal I. Photo: Korean-Nepalese Friendship Expedition 2024

Annapurna trails closed

Several Nepal trails remain closed due to landslides. Because of contradictory information on social media, trekkers should verify with local outfitters or tourism boards. While the Manaslu Circuit is open, landslides have severely affected the Manang region in general and the Annapurna Circuit in particular. Meanwhile, an avalanche cut the Thorong La, the highest point of the Annapurna trail. Check yesterday’s images, below.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Nepal’s National Trust for Nature Conservation said today that trekking permits for Annapurna are available again, but area trekkers reported that several major landslides have seriously damaged even the Annapurna South Side Base Camp trek. There are power outages and no cell connection.

“As of now [October 1], above Manang, everything is closed,” trekker Krishna Acharya has just posted on Facebook’s Annapurna Circuit Trek group.

The change of plans of even this hardcore Italian team suggests that the area is not yet suitable for trekking.

title: Germany Returns Over 800 Historic Nepali Documents Dating Back to 13th Century - INDIA New England News
description: Germany Returns Over 800 Historic Nepali Documents Dating Back to 13th Century  INDIA New England News
publisher.title: INDIA New England News
full_article:
Kathmandu – More than 800 historical documents, including manuscripts dating back to the 13th century, have been returned to Nepal from Germany, marking a significant recovery of the country’s cultural and historical heritage.

The collection, which includes ancient palm-leaf manuscripts, royal decrees, court orders, legal records, Sanskrit texts and historical travel accounts, was formally handed over to the National Archives of Nepal on Friday, according to the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The documents were previously held in the private collection of the late Joseph Peter Rindfleisch. His son, Walter Rindfleisch, transferred the collection to Professor Axel Michaels of the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, who coordinated its return to Nepal.

Michaels, along with researchers Manik Bajracharya and Rajan Khatiwada, handed over the documents to Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal during a ceremony in Kathmandu.

According to the Foreign Ministry, the collection contains materials gathered from Nepal between the 1780s and the 1990s, providing valuable insights into the country’s political, legal, intellectual and cultural history.

The collection includes 465 palm-leaf manuscripts from the Malla period, including royal decrees bearing red seals, and 312 legal decrees and royal documents from the Shah and Rana periods. It also contains 18 manuscripts and travel diaries from the offices of Rana prime ministers and 11 manuscripts covering various subjects.

Some of the palm-leaf manuscripts are among Nepal’s oldest surviving historical documents.

Speaking at the handover ceremony, Khanal described the return as an important step toward restoring Nepal’s cultural rights and ownership of its historical heritage.

“Our art, literature, traditions and sacred scriptures are not merely physical remnants; they are the living soul of our civilisation. They carry centuries of philosophical thought, political governance, legal knowledge and spiritual life,” he said.

Khanal also acknowledged Joseph Peter Rindfleisch’s wish to return the documents to Nepal and praised Michaels and his research team for their work in identifying, preserving and facilitating the repatriation of the materials.

Before their return, the documents were preserved and cataloged by the Heidelberg University Library and the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities.

The repatriation was coordinated through a partnership involving Nepal’s Embassy in Germany, Heidelberg University, the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, the Saraf Foundation and Nepal’s National Archives.

Khanal noted that Nepal and Germany are both parties to the 1970 UNESCO Convention, which seeks to prevent the illegal import, export and transfer of cultural property.

He said the handover demonstrated the two countries’ commitment to protecting cultural heritage and expressed appreciation for the support provided by the German government, the German Embassy in Kathmandu and Heidelberg University.

“Today’s handover is an important example of our shared international commitment,” Khanal said. (Source: IANS)

KATHMANDU — Nepal will kick off a high-stakes effort this fiscal year to drain four glacial lakes perched high in the mountains, as it scrambles to ⁠reduce flood risks, officials said, after a recent disaster that killed more than 1,400.

Rescuers are still searching for more than 5,000 people missing in the border region with China after August’s glacier collapse unleashed landslides and a flash flood that tore through valleys.

“Our aim is to lower the risk of the lakes breaching their natural dams and reduce the risk of downstream floods,” said Subash Tuladhar, an expert with a government research centre tasked ⁠with overseeing the new project.

Canals will drain water into nearby ​rivers ⁠in a regulated way, he said, adding that workers faced health risks as a result of the lengthy periods of high-altitude work required, in addition to the dangers of sudden flooding.

Nepali Army personnel carry bodies of victims on Aug. 28. Prabin Ranabhat / AFP via Getty

Design work and detailed studies targeting the ⁠central and eastern lakes of Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho and Hongu II, will begin in the fiscal year that ​runs until ⁠mid-July 2027, authorities said.

The lakes, at heights ranging from ‌4,050 m to 5,483 m (13,280 ft to 18,000 ft), rank among Nepal’s most potentially dangerous, the United Nations Development Programme and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said in a 2020 report.

Nepal had the skills and experience required for ‌the $50-million project to be funded by the Green Climate Fund, the UNDP and ‌the government, added Tuladhar, of Nepal’s Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research.

Draining project could take six years

The work of draining “through gated structures” will start after a detailed study, and could take up to six years to complete, said Sanjeeb Baral, the Centre’s executive director.

It will encompass installation of sensors, a ⁠flood forecasting and warning system, and efforts to build downstream resilience and prepare communities for the risks.

In similar previous efforts, Nepal lowered by 3 m (10 ft) the level of the central Himalayan glacial lake of Tsho Rolpa in 2000, and that of Imja in the vicinity of Mount Everest, the world’s tallest peak, 10 years ago.

Nepal’s disaster served as a warning to the world, Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, told the United Nations in an impassioned speech last month that blamed climate change despite his country’s negligible emissions.

title: Climate justice should be put into practice: Foreign Minister Khanal - The Rising Nepal
description: Climate justice should be put into practice: Foreign Minister Khanal  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Oct 2: Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal has emphasized the need to put climate justice into practice rather than confining it to slogan.

Foreign Minister Khanal urged the international community to provide new, easily-accessible and grant-based climate finance to Nepal to cope with the crisis surfaced from climate change.

Addressing the 'Kathmandu Climate Week-2026' organised here today, he underlined that Nepal's development, agriculture, infrastructure, water security, public health, energy transition, financial stability and foreign policy are directly connected with climate change.

"Although Nepal contributes 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emission, Nepali people have had to lose lives and properties due to climate crisis. Nepal's contribution to create climate crisis is negligible. We bear a disproportionate burden of its impacts," argued the Foreign Minister.

He stressed, "The meaning of climate justice is to accept this disproportionate burden and a concrete step should be taken to address it."

Minister Khanal pointed out the need of international cooperation in adaptation support, technology transfer and institutional capacity building is essential to mitigate the damage Nepal is facing due to climate change.

He also expressed the view that the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage, established with aim of immediately providing financial resources to the countries affected by climate-induced disaster, should not be confined to the complexities of administrative procedures.

Talking about Bhotekoshi flood and landslide, he shared that the disaster occurred at mountainous region had caused huge loss of lives and properties as well as made serious impact on road, bridge, hydropower, infrastructures and livelihood of local community.

Minister Khanal mentioned that climate-related disasters have created structural obstacles in Nepal's development process. He pointed out that it is concerning that the limited resources allocated for development often have to be spent repeatedly on rescue, rehabilitation, and reconstruction after disasters.

He emphasized that roads, bridges, electricity transmission lines, and urban settlements should be built to withstand climate-related risks for at least 20 to 30 years, keeping the risks of climate change in mind.

Similarly, Minister Khanal pointed out the need to reduce the gap between scientific research and policy decisions, emphasizing that data from studies on glacier melting and the state of glacial lakes should be quickly transformed into effective early warning systems.

He said that such a system should be able to deliver information in time to farmers at risk and residents of remote areas.

The Foreign Minister emphasized that government institutions need to be strengthened for the effective use of climate finance, and since climate-related risks are cross-border in nature, scientific cooperation with neighboring countries should also be expanded.

He mentioned that to protect the shared river system and reduce disaster risks, it is necessary to exchange water and weather-related data from the time without political influence with neighboring countries.

Foreign Minister Khanal shared that a Climate Diplomacy Section has been set up in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to make Nepal's role in international climate change talks more effective.

He said that the structure would link Nepal's internal climate realities with international negotiations, making Nepal's diplomatic efforts more integrated, consistent, and active.

Referring to the Himalayas as the 'Third Pole,' Minister Khanal said that the water flowing from its glaciers affects the lives of about two billion people in the downstream areas and emphasized that protecting the Himalayas is not just important for Nepal but is a key part of global ecological security.

Minister Khanal expressed the view that Nepal's voice on the international stage, in view of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP-31) and the mid-term review of the Doha Work Programme should be based on the real experiences of communities, scientific evidence, and practical solutions.(RSS)

The Archdiocese of Los Angeles announced Friday that parishes and Catholic schools will take up special collections Sunday and Oct. 11 to assist victims of deadly flooding and landslides in Nepal.

The emergency collections will assist people affected by an Aug. 26 glacial outburst flood and landslide in the Nepal-Tibet border region, according to the archdiocese.

The disaster unleashed flash floods and debris flows across northern Nepal, sweeping away villages and destroying homes, schools, hospitals and other infrastructure, the archdiocese said.

Nearly 1.6 million people have been affected, more than 1,400 have been confirmed dead, more than 5,600 remain missing and thousands have been injured.
